narrative:
The model estimates your chance of failing the final year at 25%, meaning roughly a one-in-four risk and a three-in-four chance of passing. That is a warning rather than a certainty, but under the school’s decision rule it is enough to require remedial courses so that a moderate risk is not left unaddressed.

The three most influential signals in your profile all pushed the estimate toward passing, not failing. The strongest was your record of no past class failures, which matches the average for students who passed. The second was your intention to continue to higher education; all passing students in the comparison shared that goal. The third was your family size of three or fewer, which also leaned toward passing, although larger families are more common among passers. These strengths are why the estimated fail risk is only 25%, rather than higher. The overall flag comes from other parts of your profile: you report studying less than two hours weekly, high weekend alcohol consumption and frequent going out, all of which are less common among students who pass.

To improve your position, protect the strengths the model recognised: keep your failure count at zero and keep your higher-education goal. Increase weekly study time, reduce weekend alcohol use and going out, and use support from your mother or school when available. Keeping absences low will also help.
